Air pollution, traffic accidents, and groundwater depletion share one feature. Whoever causes the damage does not pay for it. Environmental and resource economics calls this an externality. Governments respond with traffic rules, infrastructure, subsidies, zoning, and certification programs. Whether these policies work, and what else they change, is an important empirical question. My research evaluates them with causal inference and population-wide administrative data from Taiwan, and the results often differ from what the policy assumed. Externalities arise not only from factory chimneys but also on farmland and city streets, so my work follows two connected lines. The first asks whether environmental practices on farms can also raise farm income. The second asks how traffic rules, infrastructure, fares, and large events change accidents and emissions.

## 1. Agricultural Production and the Environment

Practices that lower farm income are unlikely to spread, so this line of work asks whether environmental goals and farm income can go together.

Solar power needs land, but panels on farmland raise concerns about competition with agriculture. Rooftop panels use no farmland. Using the 2020 agriculture census, we find that livestock and poultry farms with rooftop panels have higher sales [@liou2025rooftop], and chicken farms sell 5.8% more, mainly through higher output [@lee2025solar]. The government also zones fish ponds for aquavoltaics. Farmland prices rose 13.5% after land entered these zones, which likely reflects the value of the development rights [@chang2027aquavoltaics].

The more widespread environmental effect of farming comes from chemical fertilizer and pesticide, which are hard to regulate because they come from many dispersed sources. Food traceability systems target food safety, yet we find that adopting farms are 8.2, 15.4, and 40 percentage points less likely to use chemical fertilizer, pesticide, and groundwater, and their revenue also rises [@chang2026food]. Not every environmental practice raises income. Forest farms with greater tree diversity earn less on average, but their revenue is much more stable [@lee2025forest]. Such practices can thus benefit farmers through lower risk.

## 2. Transportation, Mobility, and Externalities

Traffic produces two main externalities, accidents and emissions. Public transit is often seen as a way to reduce both, so I first examine what changes transit use. Taiwan never imposed a COVID-19 lockdown, yet each new confirmed case reduced Taipei Metro ridership by 1.43%, so perceived risk alone changed travel behavior [@chang2021metro]. On the policy side, the Taipei monthly pass raised metro ridership by 4.3% [@liou2025monthly]. Emissions fall only if 70% to 80% of new trips replace car or motorcycle trips.

Most trips still rely on motor vehicles, so road safety depends on rules and infrastructure. After part of Tainan City removed the two-stage left turn rule for motorcycles, accidents fell 21% [@liou2026hookturn]. Counterintuitive rules can raise accident risk. Taiwan's nationwide intersection upgrade reduced injury crashes by 8.2% and pedestrian crashes by 14.8%, and each NT$1 spent saved about NT$3.5 in medical costs [@liou2027ppi].

Beyond daily travel, large events bring sudden surges of traffic. Air quality fell 17.5% during the Hakka Tomb-Sweeping Day. Previous studies attributed holiday pollution to incense, joss paper, and fireworks, but we find that the main cause is greater motor vehicle use [@chang2024air]. During the Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage, accidents rose 14.9%, and 9.8% even in neighboring townships off the route [@liou2026religious].

## 3. Consumption and Markets

I also examine how markets respond to external shocks. During the pandemic, consumers moved food purchases online [@liou2024covid]. After the pandemic, hotel revenue recovered through higher room rates rather than more guests [@liou2026hotel]. When the hog auction market closes for festivals, traded quantities fall by about 12% around the closure and price volatility rises sharply [@lee2026hog]. A strategic trade model also shows that the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism promotes green investment by exporters [@liou2025cbam].

## 4. Dissertation and Work in Progress

My dissertation, *The Environmental Economics of Urban Transport: Three Essays on Fare Policy, Vehicle Electrification, and Transit Disruption in Taiwan*, extends the second line. It studies three ways in which policies and events change travel behavior and emissions. The first essay is the monthly pass study above [@liou2025monthly]. The second essay uses a national survey of taxi drivers to compare the revenue, costs, and carbon emissions of electric and gasoline taxis. The third essay examines the random attack on the Taipei Metro in December 2025. No line or station was closed, yet ridership fell 2.9% in the following month.

Including the second essay, eight papers are under revision, under review, or in preparation for submission. Three are under revision. They study the adoption of environmentally controlled housing and the distribution of farm revenue (Technological Forecasting and Social Change), whether consumption vouchers benefit agricultural cooperatives (Food Policy), and the effects of ecosystem investment on rural housing markets and farming communities (Ecosystem Services). Two are under review. They study forest restoration and the financial performance of firms, and how cleaner air and smaller compensation transfers are both reflected in housing prices after a coal-reduction policy at the Taichung Power Plant. Besides the taxi study, two papers in preparation study a pension reform and succession on family farms, and the housing gains and traffic-safety costs around the stations of the Taoyuan Airport Metro.

## 5. Future Research

Over the next three to five years, I will continue along these two lines. Each project starts from a paper in progress and from data that I have already assembled. On agricultural production and the environment, I will use the rice production cost survey and rice revenue insurance records to compare organic and conventional rice in revenue, yield variability, and carbon emissions. I will also study the risks and multiple benefits of carbon credits from agriculture and forestry.

On transportation, I have built a nationwide grid-by-month panel of traffic accidents. I will use it to evaluate how working-hour rules for food delivery platforms affect accidents. I also plan to compare how different security incidents and protective measures change the demand for public transit. In addition, I will use property transaction records to study how public infrastructure and better environmental quality are reflected in housing prices.

I will apply for National Science and Technology Council grants with these projects and involve students in research with administrative data from Taiwan. On farms and in cities, my research asks who responds, by how much, and who bears the costs and benefits when a policy or shock changes the cost of harming the environment or the reward for improving it.
